lessonTitle: Recognising Dying, Advance Care Planning and Communication

blocks.text: Over four days a 69-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer has stopped getting out of bed, takes only sips, sleeps most of the day and has a mottled, cool lower limb. His wife asks quietly, 'Is he dying?' How do you decide, and what should change in his care as a result?

blocks.markdown: Caring for a dying person well depends on recognising that death is likely in the next hours to days, because that recognition changes what we do: we stop interventions that no longer help, treat distressing symptoms promptly, support the family, and plan for the place and manner of death. In England, NICE guideline NG31 (care of dying adults in the last days of life) and NG142 (end of life care for adults: service delivery) set out expectations, and the former 'Liverpool Care Pathway' was replaced by individualised care. This unit covers three skills: recognising dying and reviewing treatment (objective 1), advance care planning (objective 2), and breaking bad news and supporting those who grieve (objective 3).

blocks.title: The dying phase and individualised care
blocks.text: The **last days of life** is the period in which death is expected within hours or days; some definitions extend to about the last two to three days. Recognition is a **multidisciplinary clinical judgement**, not a single sign. **Advance care planning (ACP)** is a voluntary process of discussion between a person and those who care for them about their future wishes, which may be recorded. **Individualised care** means a documented plan that reflects the person's needs, preferences and the views of those important to them, reviewed regularly.

blocks.markdown: **Recognising the dying patient.** Think of the dying phase when a person with advanced illness, or after an acute event with no response to treatment, shows several of the following: progressive weakness and increased time in bed, profound fatigue, reduced intake of food and fluid and difficulty swallowing, increasing drowsiness, withdrawal, change in breathing pattern (Cheyne-Stokes breathing, apnoeic pauses), noisy respiratory secretions, peripheral cooling and mottling, and reduced urine output. No single sign is reliable. First **exclude reversible causes** of deterioration (for example infection, hypercalcaemia, opioid toxicity, retention, dehydration, drug interactions) and ask whether the change is consistent with the expected illness trajectory. Involve the senior clinician and the multidisciplinary team, check that the person and those important to them are told clearly, and revisit the judgement if the person improves; people sometimes rally.

headers: Typical change when dying (individualised, not automatic)
rows: Are they still useful? What is the time to benefit?
Stop non-essential medicines (for example statins, supplements, many antihypertensives); continue those that relieve symptoms, such as analgesia, anti-emetic and antiepileptic if needed
Can the person still swallow safely?
Change to a non-oral route (often subcutaneous) when swallowing fails; a continuous subcutaneous infusion may be used
Are there prescribed doses for pain, agitation, noisy secretions, nausea and breathlessness?
Prescribe in advance to avoid delay in relief; doses must be checked against the current BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance
Stop routine blood tests, observations and measurements that do not change care; continue symptom review
What does the person want, and what do they benefit from?
Offer support for oral intake and mouth care; consider clinically assisted hydration if it may help, as a time-limited trial reviewed regularly, rather than automatically providing or withholding
Would CPR succeed or be wanted?
Make and record a resuscitation decision (DNACPR/ReSPECT); discuss with the person or those close to them
blocks.caption: Reviewing treatment in the last days of life. Each row is a prompt for an individual decision.

blocks.title: Reviewing a drug chart in the last days of life
blocks.prompt: A 69-year-old man is judged to be dying of metastatic pancreatic cancer. His chart lists simvastatin, aspirin, ramipril, laxative, modified-release morphine, an oral anti-emetic and omeprazole. He can no longer swallow tablets. Suggest a rational review.

steps.text: Ask which drugs relieve symptoms or prevent distressing events in the next days. Statin, aspirin and ramipril offer no benefit within days and may be stopped; discuss with the patient or his family and document.

Keep symptom control. Pain and nausea must remain controlled, so convert the opioid and anti-emetic to a route that works, usually subcutaneous, by a continuous infusion with breakthrough doses; the doses must be calculated carefully and checked against the current BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance, with specialist palliative care advice if unsure.

Consider the rest: stop the oral laxative if no longer taking food but review bowel needs, and check for urinary retention or constipation as reversible causes of restlessness; stop omeprazole if no clear symptomatic benefit.
Prescribe anticipatory medicines for pain, agitation or delirium, noisy respiratory secretions, nausea and breathlessness, with clear indications and maximum doses.
Communicate and record: explain the changes to him and his wife, document the reasons, and review daily.

blocks.answer: The review keeps only treatments that relieve symptoms, changes the route as swallowing fails and ensures anticipatory medicines are prescribed, individualised and checked against current references.

blocks.markdown: **Advance care planning (objective 2).** ACP is a process rather than a form. A good conversation explores what the person understands about their illness, what matters most to them, their hopes and fears, preferences for care, preferred place of care and death, and who should speak for them. Its main outputs include: a record of **preferences and wishes**; an **advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT)** where the person wants to refuse specified treatment in specified circumstances; appointment of a **Lasting Power of Attorney (health and welfare)**; and a **treatment escalation and resuscitation plan**. In the UK, the **ReSPECT** process (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment) records a person's priorities and clinical recommendations for emergency care, including resuscitation, and the **DNACPR** (do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation) decision is one possible recommendation within it. A DNACPR decision applies **only to CPR**; it does not mean 'do not treat'. Plans should be shared across services (for example with the GP and the ambulance service), reviewed when circumstances change, and respected when the person has capacity or a valid decision exists. Under the Mental Capacity Act, a person with capacity may refuse CPR; if a person lacks capacity, a best-interests decision and consultation are required.

blocks.title: Having an ACP conversation
blocks.prompt: Mrs Gill, 81, has advanced heart failure with three admissions in six months. She is clear and well. Outline the structure of an ACP conversation and what you would document.

steps.text: Prepare and invite: choose a calm time, check she wants to talk and who she wants present, and review her records, including any previous decisions.
Explore understanding and values: ask what she understands about her heart condition, what worries her, and what would make a good day or a bad day.

Share information honestly: explain in plain language that the illness is progressive, with uncertainty about timing, and what treatments can and cannot do, including CPR success rates in advanced heart failure (individualised, not quoted from memory).
Elicit preferences: for place of care, hospital admission, CPR, and whether she wishes to appoint an attorney or write an ADRT. Respond to emotion and avoid leading her.

Document and share: record her wishes and any ReSPECT recommendations with her agreement, give her a copy, share with the GP and relevant teams, and plan to review. If she lacks capacity in future, her recorded wishes inform best interests.

blocks.answer: ACP is a person-centred process that produces documented preferences and, where wanted, ReSPECT recommendations, an ADRT and an LPA, shared and reviewed over time.

blocks.markdown: **Breaking bad news and supporting families (objective 3).** Good communication reduces distress and complaints. The **SPIKES** framework is widely taught: **S**etting (private, seated, interruptions minimised, key people present); **P**erception (ask what the patient already understands); **I**nvitation (ask how much they want to know); **K**nowledge (give a warning shot, then short chunks in plain language, avoiding jargon and euphemism, checking understanding); **E**motions (acknowledge and respond with empathy; silence is allowed); **S**trategy and summary (plan the next steps, summarise, offer follow-up). For the family of a dying patient, tell them clearly that he is dying and what to expect (more sleep, change in breathing, secretions), explain what you are doing to keep him comfortable, ask what matters to them, and give practical information about visiting, staying overnight and who to contact. After death, explain the next steps and offer bereavement information.

items: Normal grief varies widely: sadness, anger, guilt, yearning, sleep and appetite disturbance, and sometimes hearing or seeing the person.
Anticipatory grief may begin before death and is also normal.
Most bereaved people cope with family, friends and community support; offer information about local bereavement services.
Persistent, disabling grief that does not ease over many months, or features of depression or suicidal thoughts, warrants assessment and referral; check current criteria and local pathways.

blocks.title: Recognise, review, communicate
blocks.text: Recognising dying is a team judgement that triggers an individualised plan: stop what no longer helps, treat symptoms, use a reliable route, prescribe anticipatory medicines, discuss resuscitation, and communicate honestly with the patient and those close to them. Document every decision and its reasoning. Check all doses against the current BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance.

blocks.title: Avoid these pitfalls
blocks.text: Do not label someone as dying without excluding reversible causes. Do not treat a DNACPR decision as a refusal of other treatment. Do not withhold information from the family out of discomfort, and do not offer euphemisms that leave them confused. Do not stop fluids or feeding by routine: decisions should be individual, discussed and reviewed.

points: Recognising the dying phase is a multidisciplinary judgement based on several signs, after excluding reversible causes; review it if the patient improves.
In the last days, review medicines against symptom benefit, change route when swallowing fails, prescribe anticipatory medicines and make an individualised, documented plan.
Advance care planning is a voluntary, ongoing conversation whose outputs can include recorded preferences, an ADRT, an LPA and a ReSPECT recommendation; DNACPR applies to CPR only.
Breaking bad news uses a structure such as SPIKES; families need clear information, emotional support and bereavement signposting.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman with end-stage COPD has deteriorated over three days: she is bedbound, barely drinking, increasingly drowsy and has mottled knees. Which should be done before concluding that she is dying?

options.text: Stop all observations and medications immediately
Wait seven days before telling the family anything
Exclude reversible causes such as infection, opioid toxicity, retention or electrolyte disturbance and seek a senior opinion
Treat mottling as a definitive sign of death within hours

questions.correctOptionText: Exclude reversible causes such as infection, opioid toxicity, retention or electrolyte disturbance and seek a senior opinion

distractorRationale.a: Symptom-relieving medicines should continue and monitoring should be tailored, not simply stopped.
distractorRationale.b: Delaying communication denies the family time to prepare.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: recognition is a team judgement made after considering reversible contributors.
distractorRationale.d: Mottling is supportive but not a definitive predictor on its own.

questions.explanation: Recognition of dying should follow a review of reversible causes and a senior, multidisciplinary judgement, with reassessment if the patient improves. Once the decision is made, the family are told and care is individualised.

questions.stem: A man judged to be dying can no longer swallow, and has been receiving oral morphine for pain. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue effective analgesia by a non-oral route, with doses calculated and checked against the BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance
Stop the opioid because he cannot swallow
Continue to give tablets and wait for him to swallow
Replace the opioid with a statin

questions.correctOptionText: Continue effective analgesia by a non-oral route, with doses calculated and checked against the BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: symptom control continues and the route changes.
distractorRationale.b: Stopping analgesia would leave pain uncontrolled.
distractorRationale.c: Forcing tablets risks aspiration and does not deliver reliable analgesia.
distractorRationale.d: A statin has no analgesic role and no value in the last days.

questions.explanation: When swallowing fails, essential symptom-relieving medicines are converted to an alternative route, commonly subcutaneous. Conversion arithmetic must be double-checked and referenced to current guidance, with palliative care advice if uncertain.

questions.stem: Which set of symptoms is routinely covered by anticipatory prescribing in the last days of life?

options.text: Hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, osteoporosis, constipation and acne
Fever, rash, itching, cough and alopecia
Insomnia, headache, indigestion, backache and anaemia
Pain, agitation, noisy respiratory secretions, nausea and vomiting, and breathlessness

questions.correctOptionText: Pain, agitation, noisy respiratory secretions, nausea and vomiting, and breathlessness

distractorRationale.a: These are chronic risk-factor conditions not needing urgent symptom relief when dying.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: these are the common distressing symptoms in the dying phase.

questions.explanation: Anticipatory medicines are individually prescribed as-required medicines for the common symptoms of the dying phase so that relief is immediate. Indications, doses and routes must be clearly written and checked against current references.

questions.stem: True or false: a DNACPR decision means that active treatment such as antibiotics, analgesia or oxygen should be withheld.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A DNACPR decision applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation. All other appropriate care and treatment continue to be offered according to the person's needs and wishes, which may be documented in a ReSPECT plan.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with motor neurone disease and capacity says he wishes to die at home and does not want CPR or hospital admission for chest infections. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Record nothing, since he can speak for himself
Document his wishes in an advance care plan or ReSPECT form with his agreement, share it with the GP and other services, and review it
Ask his family to decide instead
Tell him that preferences cannot be recorded until he loses capacity

questions.correctOptionText: Document his wishes in an advance care plan or ReSPECT form with his agreement, share it with the GP and other services, and review it

distractorRationale.a: Without a record, his wishes may be unknown in an emergency.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: wishes expressed while able should be recorded and shared so they can be followed later.
distractorRationale.c: He has capacity, so the decision is his.
distractorRationale.d: Planning ahead is most valuable while the person can take part.

questions.explanation: ACP aims to record a person's values and preferences while they can express them and to share them with those who may need to act. Review is needed if circumstances or wishes change.

questions.stem: In the SPIKES framework, what is the purpose of the 'Perception' step?

options.text: To announce the diagnosis in a single sentence
To summarise the follow-up plan
To check that interpreters are present
To ask the patient what they already understand about their illness

questions.correctOptionText: To ask the patient what they already understand about their illness

distractorRationale.a: Giving information is the Knowledge step, after a warning shot.
distractorRationale.b: Strategy and summary is the final step.
distractorRationale.c: Setting involves arranging practical conditions, not perception.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: this step identifies existing understanding and expectations.

questions.explanation: Perception asks what the patient or family already know and expect so that you can correct misunderstandings and pitch the information appropriately. It comes before the Invitation and Knowledge steps.

questions.stem: Six weeks after her husband's death from cancer, a 78-year-old woman cries daily, sleeps poorly and sometimes hears his voice, but eats, cares for herself and sees friends. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: As a psychotic illness needing antipsychotic treatment
As within the range of normal grief, with support and information about bereavement services offered
As established prolonged grief disorder
As evidence that the family were not told the diagnosis

questions.correctOptionText: As within the range of normal grief, with support and information about bereavement services offered

distractorRationale.a: Brief hearing or sensing the lost person is typically not psychosis.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: intense feelings and transient perceptual experiences of the deceased are common in normal grief, with preserved function.
distractorRationale.c: Prolonged grief is diagnosed after longer, disabling symptoms, not at six weeks with preserved function.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the history suggests this.

questions.explanation: Normal grief varies and may include sadness, sleep disturbance and sensing the person, especially early on. Assessment and referral are needed when grief is persistent and disabling, when there are features of depression or when she is at risk.

questions.stem: A son asks whether his father, who is now unconscious and has a few sips of water a day, should be given a drip. Which response best reflects good practice?

options.text: State that fluids are always withheld in the last days
State that a drip is always required to avoid suffering
Explain that the decision is individual: discuss potential benefits and burdens, consider clinically assisted hydration as a time-limited trial if it may help, and review
Refuse to discuss, as it is the doctor's decision alone

questions.correctOptionText: Explain that the decision is individual: discuss potential benefits and burdens, consider clinically assisted hydration as a time-limited trial if it may help, and review

distractorRationale.a: Withholding by routine ignores individual benefit.
distractorRationale.b: Providing by routine ignores burdens and the individual circumstances.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: NICE-style guidance supports an individual, discussed and reviewed decision.
distractorRationale.d: Families should be involved and informed.

questions.explanation: Hydration in the dying phase is an individual clinical decision weighed against benefit, burden and the person's wishes, with regular review. Good mouth care and honest explanation address the family's distress.

questions.stem: You are asked to speak to the family of a 72-year-old man who has deteriorated and is now thought to be in the last days of life. Describe how you would conduct the conversation.
markingGuide: Prepare: know the facts, find a private seated space, choose who attends, and allow time
Ask what they understand and what they expect, and how much they want to know
Give a warning shot, then clear information in plain language that he is dying, without euphemism or jargon
Explain what to expect (sleepiness, breathing changes, secretions) and what will be done to keep him comfortable
Acknowledge emotions, allow silence, check understanding and answer questions
Discuss practical matters (visiting, staying, contacts), agree a plan and follow-up, and document the conversation
questions.explanation: Using a structure such as SPIKES allows honest, compassionate communication. Clarity avoids confusion and supports the family before and after the death.

questions.stem: Describe how care changes when a patient is recognised as being in the last days of life, and explain the role of advance care planning in that situation.
markingGuide: Recognition is a senior, multidisciplinary judgement after excluding reversible causes and is reviewed regularly
Review and stop non-essential treatments and investigations; keep symptom-relieving medicines
Change to a reliable route (often subcutaneous) as swallowing fails, with doses calculated and checked against the BNF, Palliative Care Formulary and local guidance
Prescribe individualised anticipatory medicines for pain, agitation, secretions, nausea and breathlessness
Make individualised decisions about hydration and nutrition, mouth care, resuscitation and place of care
ACP informs this plan: preferences, ReSPECT recommendations, any valid ADRT and attorney's role are checked and followed
Communicate with the patient and family and document decisions, reviewing them as circumstances change
questions.explanation: In the last days, care is centred on comfort, communication and individual decisions, guided by what the person has said about their wishes. Advance care planning makes those wishes known and actionable.
